subtopic_detail: Separating drug-induced inner restlessness from an urge to move relieved by walking at night
stem:
You are the resident in a community mental health clinic. A 47-year-old man with schizophrenia attends for review. He was started on risperidone 3 mg daily 5 weeks ago after a relapse and his psychotic symptoms have improved substantially.

He complains of an unpleasant urge to move his legs that he describes as a crawling feeling deep inside them. He says it is worst when he sits down in the evening and is worse still when he goes to bed, and that getting up and walking around the room relieves it almost completely until he sits again. He sleeps poorly as a result and his partner reports he kicks during sleep.

He denies feeling mentally restless or agitated during the day, and he sits comfortably through the 30 minute consultation without shifting or rocking. On examination there is no tremor, no rigidity and no bradykinesia. Haemoglobin is 128 g/L (130-180), ferritin is 22 micrograms/L (30-500), transferrin saturation is 14 per cent (15-45), and renal function and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Sits still and comfortably throughout a 30 minute consultation, no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130-180), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-500), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45), renal and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence iron replacement therapy and review the leg symptoms and iron studies in 8 weeks
options.rationale: A circadian urge to move confined to rest and the evening, relieved by walking and associated with sleep kicking, is restless legs syndrome rather than akathisia, and low ferritin with reduced transferrin saturation identifies a reversible cause. Iron replacement is first-line when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L, and correcting it frequently resolves symptoms without any change to antipsychotic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose and review the leg symptoms and mental state in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is the correct response to akathisia, but akathisia produces continuous subjective inner restlessness with observable fidgeting that does not follow a circadian pattern or resolve with walking. Reducing the dose here risks psychotic relapse without addressing the actual cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence propranolol at a low dose and review the leg symptoms and mental state in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Propranolol is a recognised treatment for akathisia but has no established role in restless legs syndrome. It would be appropriate if the patient described generalised inner restlessness present throughout the day with visible motor manifestations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence benztropine at a low dose and review the leg symptoms and mental state in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, and examination shows no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia to support either. Benztropine is notably ineffective for akathisia as well, so it does not fit any of the plausible drug-induced alternatives here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a dopamine agonist at a low dose and review the leg symptoms and iron studies in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are effective in restless legs syndrome but carry a substantial risk of augmentation with long-term use and would also antagonise the antipsychotic effect being relied on. They are reserved for persistent symptoms after iron has been replaced and non-dopaminergic options considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Akathisia and restless legs syndrome are confused constantly in psychiatric practice because both produce an urge to move in someone taking a dopamine antagonist, and getting the distinction right determines whether an effective antipsychotic is unnecessarily reduced. Restless legs syndrome follows a circadian pattern that worsens in the evening and at rest, is relieved by movement, and is focused on the legs, whereas akathisia is present throughout the day, is experienced as generalised mental restlessness as much as physical, and is not relieved by walking. Periodic limb movements during sleep accompany restless legs syndrome in the majority of cases and are a useful collateral clue from a bed partner. Iron deficiency is the most important reversible contributor, and the treatment threshold uses a ferritin considerably higher than that used for anaemia because brain iron status is the relevant variable. Dopamine antagonists can certainly unmask or worsen restless legs syndrome, so the two conditions can coexist with the same precipitant.
key_points: Circadian worsening at rest and in the evening with relief on movement indicates restless legs syndrome
Akathisia is continuous, generalised and subjectively mental as well as motor, and is not relieved by walking
Periodic limb movements reported by a bed partner support restless legs syndrome
Replace iron when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent
Dopamine agonists risk augmentation and are not first-line despite their efficacy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for treating restless legs syndrome is below 75 micrograms/L, far above the threshold used to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia, because central nervous system iron availability rather than red cell production is the target.

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia developing weeks after starting an antidepressant in an older adult on a thiazide
stem:
You are the resident in a general medical clinic. A 76-year-old woman is referred after routine bloods taken by her general practitioner showed a low sodium. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily 4 weeks ago for a first depressive episode and reports her mood is beginning to lift.

She complains of feeling unsteady and having had one fall at home without injury. She has had no seizures, no vomiting and no confusion noted by her daughter. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, started 6 years ago, and no other medicines.

She drinks about 1.5 L of fluid daily and has not changed this. On examination she is alert and oriented, mucous membranes are moist, jugular venous pressure is not elevated, there is no peripheral oedema and postural blood pressure drop is 6 mmHg. Sodium is 124 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits. Her sodium 3 months ago was 138 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mucous membranes moist, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, postural blood pressure drop 6 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L; thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits; sodium 138 mmol/L three months ago
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 50 mg daily for 4 weeks, hydrochlorothiazide for 6 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the hydrochlorothiazide, restrict fluid intake and recheck the serum sodium within the week
options.rationale: Thiazides are a classic cause of hyponatraemia and would be the answer if the timing fitted, but she has taken it for 6 years with a normal sodium 3 months ago. It would be the correct target if the antidepressant were long-established and the diuretic recently started. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the sertraline, restrict fluid intake and recheck the serum sodium within the week
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the temporal link to a drug started 4 weeks ago in a normonatraemic patient identifies the culprit. Serotonergic antidepressants characteristically cause this within the first few weeks, most commonly in older women, and stopping the drug with fluid restriction corrects it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence intravenous hypertonic saline, restrict fluid intake and recheck the serum sodium within hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures, coma or marked confusion, and rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination. It would be indicated if she presented with a seizure or a depressed level of consciousness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence intravenous isotonic saline, continue current medicines and recheck the serum sodium within the week
options.rationale: Isotonic saline treats hypovolaemic hyponatraemia but can worsen sodium in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, because the salt is excreted while the water is retained. It would be correct if she were clinically volume deplete with a low urine sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch the sertraline to a tricyclic antidepressant, restrict fluid intake and recheck the sodium within the week
options.rationale: Tricyclics also cause the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis and add anticholinergic and cardiac conduction risks that are poorly tolerated in this age group. A switch would be considered later, to an agent such as mirtazapine or agomelatine, after the sodium has normalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Drug-induced hyponatraemia in older adults is common, underdiagnosed and frequently attributed to the wrong agent because patients typically take several implicated drugs at once. The diagnostic framework is unchanged regardless of the culprit: confirm true hypo-osmolality, assess volume status clinically, and use paired serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium to separate the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis from hypovolaemia and from renal salt wasting. Thyroid and adrenal insufficiency must be excluded because both mimic it exactly. Attribution then rests on timing, and a documented normal sodium before the new drug is the single most valuable piece of evidence, which is why baseline electrolytes before starting an antidepressant in an older patient are worth the trouble. Serotonergic agents typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks, and risk is substantially higher with advanced age, female sex, low body weight and concurrent diuretic use, all of which compound here.
key_points: Confirm hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia and assess volume status before attributing a cause
Urine osmolality above 100 mmol/kg with urine sodium above 30 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient indicates inappropriate antidiuresis
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, which mimic the syndrome
Serotonergic antidepressants typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks
Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly; hypertonic saline is only for severe neurological symptoms
explanation.pearls: Check electrolytes at baseline and again about 2 weeks after starting a serotonergic antidepressant in anyone over 65, particularly if they also take a thiazide, because the fall is usually asymptomatic until sodium drops below about 125 mmol/L.

subtopic_detail: Selecting a replacement antipsychotic after a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval
stem:
You are the registrar in an inpatient psychiatric unit. A 52-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has been taking haloperidol 10 mg daily for 3 weeks with good symptomatic response after a relapse with command hallucinations.

A routine electrocardiogram taken this morning shows sinus rhythm at 68 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, repeated and confirmed on a second recording. His admission electrocardiogram 3 weeks ago showed a corrected QT interval of 432 ms.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no chest pain. He takes no other medicines and denies illicit substance use, and a urine drug screen is negative. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid function normal and renal and liver function within normal limits. There is no family history of sudden death or of unexplained drowning. Echocardiography shows structurally normal heart with normal systolic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 68/min, corrected QT interval 512 ms confirmed on repeat, versus 432 ms on admission. Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid, renal and liver function within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative. Echocardiogram structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the haloperidol dose to 5 mg daily, repeating the electrocardiogram after the reduction
options.rationale: Although the effect is dose-related, continuing the same agent above a corrected QT interval of 500 ms leaves the patient exposed to arrhythmia for the sake of convenience. Dose reduction would be a reasonable response to a modest prolongation in the 460 to 500 ms range with close monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence ziprasidone, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: Ziprasidone produces greater corrected QT prolongation than most other antipsychotics, so substituting it exchanges one repolarisation risk for a similar or larger one. The near-pair point is that both are effective antipsychotics but they sit at opposite ends of the repolarisation risk spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence aripiprazole, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms carries a materially increased risk of torsades de pointes and requires the offending agent to be stopped rather than continued at a lower dose. Aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of the available antipsychotics, making it the rational replacement when antipsychotic cover must continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence citalopram, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: Citalopram is an antidepressant with its own dose-dependent corrected QT prolongation and would leave the psychotic symptoms untreated. An antidepressant might be added later for the affective component once an antipsychotic with a favourable cardiac profile is established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue haloperidol and give intravenous magnesium sulfate, repeating the electrocardiogram afterward
options.rationale: Magnesium is the treatment for established torsades de pointes and for correcting hypomagnesaemia, and this patient's magnesium is already normal with no arrhythmia. It would be given immediately if he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated corrected QT prolongation is a genuine but often mismanaged risk, and the practical decisions turn on two numbers: an absolute corrected QT interval above 500 ms, or an increase of more than 60 ms from baseline, both of which mark a materially elevated arrhythmia risk. This patient meets both. Before attributing the change to the drug, reversible contributors must be corrected, since hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia and hypothyroidism all prolong repolarisation and are far easier to fix than a psychotropic regimen. Antipsychotics differ substantially in this effect, with haloperidol, particularly intravenously, and ziprasidone among the higher risk agents, while aripiprazole, lurasidone and brexpiprazole have minimal effect. Because untreated psychosis carries its own substantial mortality, the answer is almost never to stop antipsychotic treatment altogether but to move to an agent with a better repolarisation profile and repeat the electrocardiogram once the new drug is at steady state.
key_points: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline requires action
Correct potassium, magnesium, calcium and thyroid abnormalities before attributing prolongation to a drug
Haloperidol and ziprasidone are higher risk; aripiprazole and lurasidone have minimal effect
Stopping all antipsychotic treatment is rarely correct given the mortality of untreated psychosis
Repeat the electrocardiogram once the replacement agent reaches steady state
explanation.pearls: Intravenous haloperidol prolongs the corrected QT interval considerably more than the oral route at equivalent doses, which is why continuous cardiac monitoring is advised whenever it is given intravenously for acute behavioural disturbance.

subtopic_detail: New onset misidentification delusion with fluctuating attention in an older adult
stem:
You are the registrar called to see a 74-year-old man on a medical ward. He was admitted 3 days ago for management of cellulitis and is improving on intravenous antibiotics.

Overnight he became distressed and told nursing staff that his wife of 45 years has been replaced by an impostor who looks identical to her. He accepts that the woman visiting resembles his wife in every respect but insists she is a different person, and he has asked staff to call the police.

He has no prior psychiatric history. His daughter reports that over the past 8 months he has been seeing small animals in the lounge room that are not there, has become noticeably slower and more stooped, and has had days when he is sharp and days when he is barely rousable in his chair. His sleep has been disrupted for over a year by shouting and thrashing during dreams. On examination there is symmetrical bradykinesia with mild cogwheel rigidity in both wrists and no resting tremor. Attention fluctuates through the interview. Sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein are within normal limits or improving, urinalysis is clear, and non-contrast computed tomography of the brain shows age-related atrophy only.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia with mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, no resting tremor, fluctuating attention through the interview
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid function, full blood count and C-reactive protein within normal limits or improving; urinalysis clear; non-contrast computed tomography of the brain shows age-related atrophy only
data_table.Collateral: Eight months of visual hallucinations of small animals, progressive bradykinesia, day-to-day fluctuation in alertness; over a year of shouting and thrashing during dreams

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: An acute confusional state precipitated by the current infective illness
options.rationale: Delirium is a genuine contributor to the acute deterioration, but it does not explain 8 months of progressive parkinsonism, visual hallucinations and over a year of dream enactment reported by the family. A purely delirious picture would be correct if collateral history described normal baseline cognition and function. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A primary psychotic disorder presenting for the first time in later life
options.rationale: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis typically features persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations without parkinsonism, fluctuating attention or dream enactment. It would be the diagnosis if motor signs and cognitive fluctuation were absent and cognition were otherwise preserved. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A neurodegenerative disorder characterised by cortical tau and amyloid deposition
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease presents with prominent early episodic memory loss and does not typically produce early parkinsonism, marked cognitive fluctuation or dream enactment behaviour. The near-pair distinction is that both cause dementia with psychotic features, but visual hallucinations and parkinsonism arise early in synucleinopathy and late in Alzheimer disease. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A neurodegenerative disorder characterised by cortical synuclein deposition
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and a long history of dream enactment together identify dementia with Lewy bodies, of which delusional misidentification is a recognised feature. The dream enactment behaviour is particularly telling, since it frequently precedes cognitive symptoms by years and is strongly predictive of an underlying synucleinopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A cerebrovascular disorder producing stepwise cognitive decline from small vessel disease
options.rationale: Vascular cognitive impairment produces stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and imaging evidence of infarction or extensive white matter disease, and this scan shows atrophy only. It would be the diagnosis with a stepwise history and corresponding vascular lesions on imaging. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

explanation.summary: Delusional misidentification, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an identical impostor, is far more often a sign of organic brain disease than of a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when it appears for the first time in later life. The task is to identify what underlies it, and the collateral history usually carries the diagnosis where the mental state examination alone cannot. Here the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder gives the core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Recognising it has immediate and serious practical consequences because severe sensitivity to antipsychotics occurs in a substantial proportion of patients and can produce irreversible parkinsonism, sedation, autonomic instability and death. Cholinesterase inhibitors, by contrast, are often strikingly effective for the hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation, so the correct diagnosis changes treatment in the opposite direction to instinct.
key_points: New misidentification delusions in later life suggest organic disease rather than primary psychiatric illness
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment define the core clinical picture
Dream enactment behaviour often precedes cognitive symptoms by years and predicts synucleinopathy
Severe antipsychotic sensitivity can cause irreversible deterioration and death
Cholinesterase inhibitors frequently improve hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation
explanation.pearls: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable in suspected Lewy body disease, quetiapine at the lowest possible dose is the conventional choice, and typical agents such as haloperidol are avoided entirely because of the risk of irreversible parkinsonism and death.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

subtopic_detail: Engaging a patient presenting to dermatology with fixed belief of skin infestation and specimen collection
stem:
You are the resident in a dermatology clinic. A 58-year-old woman attends with her fourth referral in 8 months, convinced that tiny parasites are living under her skin.

She brings a sealed container of lint, scabs and fibres collected from her bathroom floor, which she says are the organisms and their eggs. She has been applying household bleach and kerosene to her forearms and has been buying veterinary ivermectin online.

She lives alone, manages her finances and her part-time bookkeeping work without difficulty, and has no other unusual beliefs. She reports no low mood, no hallucinations in any modality, and no substance use, and a urine drug screen is negative. On examination there are multiple excoriations and two areas of secondary infection on both forearms with no burrows, no webspace involvement and no primary lesions. Microscopy of the container contents shows textile fibres and keratin debris only. Full blood count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function, glucose, B12 and human immunodeficiency virus serology are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Multiple excoriations with two areas of secondary infection on both forearms, no burrows, no webspace involvement, no primary lesions
data_table.Investigations: Microscopy of patient-collected specimen shows textile fibres and keratin debris only. Full blood count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function, glucose, B12 and human immunodeficiency virus serology within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Treat the secondary skin infection, explain that the specimen contains no parasites and discharge her from the clinic
options.rationale: Direct contradiction of a fixed delusion does not alter the belief and typically leads the patient to seek another clinician, continuing the cycle of presentations and self-treatment. Explaining negative results works where the belief is an overvalued idea held with doubt rather than a fixed delusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Treat the secondary skin infection, prescribe topical permethrin and arrange dermatology review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing an antiparasitic reinforces the delusional belief and exposes her to further unnecessary treatment while the underlying disorder progresses. Permethrin would be correct for genuine scabies, which produces burrows and webspace involvement and typically affects household contacts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Treat the secondary skin infection, arrange an involuntary psychiatric assessment under the mental health legislation
options.rationale: Involuntary assessment requires risk to the person or others that cannot be managed voluntarily, and she is functioning independently and engaging with services. It would become appropriate if self-treatment escalated to serious harm or if she refused all care while deteriorating markedly. (Source: RANZCP: Mental health legislation)

options.text: Treat the secondary skin infection, commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have a role in body dysmorphic disorder and in obsessional preoccupations held with insight, but not in a fixed delusion of infestation. An antidepressant would be added if a comorbid depressive disorder emerged alongside antipsychotic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Treat the secondary skin infection, build rapport over several visits and introduce a low dose antipsychotic
options.rationale: A single fixed delusion with preserved functioning in every other domain is delusional disorder of the somatic type, which responds to antipsychotic treatment but only if the patient accepts it. Treating the visible skin damage first and framing medication around distress and skin healing rather than around belief is what makes acceptance possible, since direct confrontation reliably ends the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation is the most common somatic delusional disorder and presents almost exclusively to dermatology and general practice rather than to mental health services, because the patient's explanatory model is dermatological. The defining feature is that the delusion is encapsulated: outside this single belief, thought form, mood, perception and social and occupational functioning are entirely intact, which is why involuntary treatment is rarely justified and why the person seems so credible. Secondary causes must be excluded first, including substance use, particularly stimulants, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia, since any of these can produce an identical picture with a different treatment. The specimen sign, in which the patient brings collected material as proof, is characteristic and should be examined seriously and microscopically rather than dismissed, because taking the complaint seriously is the foundation of any therapeutic relationship. Antipsychotics achieve substantial improvement in most patients, but only a minority of the therapeutic effort is pharmacological and the rest is engagement.
key_points: An encapsulated delusion with otherwise preserved functioning defines delusional disorder
Exclude stimulant use, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia
Examine patient-collected specimens microscopically rather than dismissing them
Direct confrontation of the belief ends the therapeutic relationship without changing it
Antipsychotics are effective, but acceptance depends on framing treatment around distress and skin healing
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about methamphetamine and prescribed stimulants before diagnosing primary delusional infestation, because stimulant-induced formication with secondary delusional elaboration resolves with abstinence and needs no long-term antipsychotic.
